tasks.description: Use `with open('test.txt', 'w') as f:` to write 'Context managers are great!' to a file. Then read it back.
tasks.hint:
The `with` statement guarantees the file is closed when the block exits — even if an error occurs.
`with open('test.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('...')`
No need to call `f.close()` — `with` handles it automatically.
tasks.solution:
with open('test.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Context managers are great!')

with open('test.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
The first `with` writes and closes the file automatically when the block ends.
The second reopens it for reading. No `close()` calls anywhere.

tasks.description: Write a context manager class `Timer` using `__enter__` and `__exit__`. It should print the elapsed time when the `with` block exits.
tasks.hint:
`__enter__` runs when entering the `with` block — record `self.start = time.time()`
`__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb)` runs on exit — print elapsed time.
Usage: `with Timer(): # some code here`
tasks.solution:
import time

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.time()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        elapsed = time.time() - self.start
        print(f'Elapsed: {elapsed:.4f} seconds')

with Timer():
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))
print(total)
tasks.walkthrough:
Entering the block records the start time. Leaving it, however that happens, runs `__exit__`, which prints the elapsed time.
The three extra parameters of `__exit__` carry exception details; they're unused here but must be declared.

tasks.description: Use `contextlib.contextmanager` to write a generator-based context manager `managed_resource()` that prints 'Acquiring' and 'Releasing'.
tasks.hint:
`from contextlib import contextmanager`
`@contextmanager def managed_resource(): print('Acquiring'); yield; print('Releasing')`
The `yield` is where the `with` block body runs.
tasks.solution:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def managed_resource():
    print('Acquiring')
    yield
    print('Releasing')

with managed_resource():
    pass
tasks.walkthrough:
The decorator turns the generator into a context manager.
Everything before `yield` runs on entry, the `with` body runs at the `yield`, and everything after runs on exit.
The body here is just `pass`, so only the two messages are printed.

tasks.description: Use a context manager to safely open a file that may not exist. Catch the FileNotFoundError and print 'File not found'.
tasks.hint:
Wrap the `with open(...)` in a `try/except FileNotFoundError:` block.
Alternatively, check existence first with `import os; os.path.exists(path)`.
The `with` statement and try/except work together cleanly.
tasks.walkthrough:
`open()` raises FileNotFoundError before the `with` block even starts.
Wrapping the whole `with` in `try` catches it and prints a friendly message.

tasks.description: Open two files simultaneously in one `with` statement: one for reading, one for writing. Copy contents from one to the other.
tasks.hint:
Python allows multiple context managers in one `with`: `with open('in.txt') as r, open('out.txt', 'w') as w:`
Inside: `w.write(r.read())` copies everything.
Both files are automatically closed when the block exits.
tasks.solution:
with open('source.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Some text to copy.\nAnd a second line.')

with open('source.txt', 'r') as reader, open('copy.txt', 'w') as writer:
    writer.write(reader.read())

with open('copy.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
The first block creates something to copy so the task runs on its own.
The middle `with` opens both files at once, reads everything from one and writes it to the other.
Both files close when that block ends.

lesson.intro:
You've been writing `with open(...) as f:` for a while. The thing that makes
`with` work is called a context manager: something that sets up when you enter
the block and cleans up when you leave, no matter how you leave. Today you'll
see how they work and write your own.

sections.heading: Why with matters
sections.body:
Without `with`, you have to remember to close the file, and if an error
happens before the `close()` line, it never runs. `with` guarantees the
cleanup.
sections.code:
with open('test.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Context managers are great!')

with open('test.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())
print(f.closed)

sections.heading: A class with __enter__ and __exit__
sections.body:
Any object with these two methods can be used in a `with`. `__enter__` runs
at the start (its return value is what `as` binds). `__exit__` runs at the
end, even if an exception happened inside the block.

sections.heading: The shortcut: @contextmanager
sections.body:
Writing a class is a lot for something simple. `contextlib.contextmanager`
turns a generator into a context manager: everything before `yield` is the
setup, everything after is the cleanup, and the `with` block runs at the
`yield`.
sections.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def managed_resource():
    print('Acquiring')
    yield
    print('Releasing')

with managed_resource():
    print('Using it')

sections.heading: Two at once, and files that might not exist
sections.body:
A single `with` can open several things, separated by commas. And `with`
doesn't catch errors for you, so wrap it in `try` if the file might be
missing.
sections.code:
with open('in.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('copy me')

with open('in.txt') as src, open('out.txt', 'w') as dst:
    dst.write(src.read())

try:
    with open('missing.txt') as f:
        print(f.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print('File not found')

watch_out: `__exit__` must accept three extra parameters (exception type, value, traceback) even if you ignore them.
In a `@contextmanager` generator, there must be exactly one `yield`.
Code after the `with` block can't use the file; it's closed. Do the reading inside.
`with` on its own doesn't handle FileNotFoundError. That's what `try`/`except` is for.
